title: An integrative reassessment of species boundaries and spatial preferences in boreal and Arctic sea spiders (Arthropoda: Pycnogonida)
text:
With Arctic ‘borealisation’, changes in the habitat preferences of shallow-water species from warmer waters are already being observed, but the effects on deep-sea fauna remain unknown. Recent studies highlight data gaps with regard to benthic biodiversity in deep Arctic waters. Sea spiders (Pycnogonida) are predatory representatives of the benthos and are more limited in their distribution potential compared to pelagic-dispersive species due to paternal brood care. Nevertheless, widespread species are present in shallow coastal regions (e.g. Pycnogonum litorale (STRØM, 1762)) as well as in deep-sea areas (e.g. Ascorhynchus abyssi SARS, 1877).



This male specimen of the deep-sea species Ascorhynchus abyssi Sars, 1877 was sampled at the geographic North Pole during the ArcWatch expedition in 2023 at a depth of 4248 m, carrying offspring on his ovigerous legs.


Uhlir et al. are working on a current inventory of the taxonomic and genetic diversity of pycnogonids in boreal, Subarctic and Arctic waters. Initial results on actual species diversity and distribution showed:

Inconsistencies in identification were found due to sexual dimorphism or regional differences.
The majority of all taxonomic morphospecies correlate with the genetic results of DNA barcoding (COI).
Selected species with a wide geographical distribution showed genetic species complexes.
Cryptic species were identified, particularly in the most species-rich genus Nymphon FABRICIUS, 1794.




Spatial overview of all projects and stations with physical samples of Pycnogonida, upon which the basis dataset will be created. The black arrow highlights the South-North sampling transect of the expeditions ALONGate 1 & 2 in 2025 and 2026, which fill knowledge gaps in the North Atlantic Gateway area.


Typical distribution areas will be summarized for each species and linked to high-resolution biotope mapping from the MAREANO program to determine species- or community-specific habitat preferences. As part of our international collaboration, the dataset comprises various projects and expeditions (ALONGate, ArcWatch, IceAGE, MAREANO, LTER HAUSGARTEN, TUNU), enabling comprehensive geographical and bathymetric coverage. The findings of this study provide fundamental information for observing shifts in distribution with which sea spiders could respond to future changes in the ocean.
This study is in preparation to submission in 2027. Stay tuned!

title: Comparing Arctic Macrobenthos Across a Decade (WCMB Talk)
text:
Macrobenthic life in the deep central Arctic Ocean is understudied despite its importance in biogeochemical cycling of carbon and nutrients. Here we focus on the Eurasian Basin that encompasses the Nansen and Amundsen Basins separated by the Gakkel Ridge. We compare macrofauna from a total of 24 box corer samples across 17 stations (3400 – 4400 m depth) in both basins sampled with RV Polarstern in 2012 and 2023. Over the last decades an increase in phytoplankton biomass at the shelves in the Arctic has been observed, but it is currently unknown if also the central Arctic is becoming more productive and if this potential surplus is translated at the benthos.
We identified 63 taxa and, as is typical, major taxonomic groups included Polychaeta followed by Bivalvia and specifically in 2023, the brooding crustaceans Isopoda, Amphipoda, Tanaidacea in the Amundsen Basin. Macrofauna density and biomass did not differ significantly between basins or the years indicating no or weak dispersal limitation by the Gakkel Ridge, consistent with previous studies. However, the population of several species sampled in 2012 consisted mostly of adults, whereas in 2023 they were made up mostly by juveniles, indicating a different status of the ecosystem despite the same time of sampling. In 2023, lower bacterial abundances and lower food quality, indicated by the proportion of chlorophyll a to total chloroplastic pigments, was observed. This difference was especially pronounced in the Amundsen Basin, where a concurrent decrease in macrofauna biomass was observed. Interestingly, Hill diversity indices were higher in 2023 compared to 2012, mostly driven by the presence of many singleton species detected in 2023.
Our results suggest differences in cryo-pelagic-benthic coupling between the years with impacts on benthic life. However, macrofauna diversity, density and biomass varied strongly among stations, reflecting deep-sea patchiness and the need for increased sampling efforts. A clear reaction of the benthos to the changing Arctic could not be observed (yet). Regular sampling across seasons is needed to understand potential multiyear changes as the benthos might respond slower in comparison to surface water communities.

title: Benthic Survey
text: The deep-sea benthos is remote and much harder to reach than shallower, coastal seafloor. We mainly uses four gears to collect our data:

title: Benthic Survey
text:
Epibenthic Sledge (EBS)
As the name suggests, EBS is similar to a trawl on the seafloor. It is optimized to capture the epifauna and infauna of the first few centimeters.
Of course, EBS leaves a trawling trail behind it and the gear itself is also sensitive to boulders on the seafloor. Therefore the EBS is only deployed at soft sediment plains and the trawling distances are normally planned between 50 to 100 meters.




dummy




EBS lifted by the winch and about to be deployed.

title: Benthic Survey
text:
Grabs
Compared to EBS, different grabs are used, also at the area where EBS is impossible to sample due to dense boulders on the seafloor. Among all of them, the Box Corer is one of the most used gear, which always brings the exact area of sediment back onboard, while keeping the sediment surface and internal structure intact. Allowing us to conduct more detailed quantitative analysis.




dummy




Box Corer is back onboard and covered by deep-sea mud.

title: Benthic Survey
text:
Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV)
The ROV is becoming a star in the deep-sea exploration. Of course we would like to work with them. ROV Phoca from GEOMAR is a very special member of us, who will bring our Benthic Lander Observatory System onto the seafloor. And if it’s not busy deploying landers, we also love to have some deep-sea “Spaziergang” with astonishing 4K cameras and our sampling boxes.
Different from EBS and grabs, as the videos of the ROV are transmitted real-time to the vessel, we can see what’s down there and sample very specifically, leaving minimal disturbance on the seafloor.




dummy




ROV Phoca ready to splash and dive

title: Benthic Survey
text:
Ocean Floor Observation System (OFOS)
Similar to ROV, OFOS is another gear based on imagery data collection. However, OFOS is for observation only - it has no manipulators, nor can it sample the seafloor. Also without any thruster, OFOS completely relied on the vessel towing it, but therefore, it’s much easier to deploy.

title: About ALONGate
text:
ALONGate is an endorsed „UN decade action“ in cooperation with DOOS and Challenger 150.


The boundary region between Iceland, Norway, and Greenland acts as a corridor for specialized fauna to extreme environmental conditions moving through the North Atlantic Gateway to the Arctic Ocean. While a huge amount of biodiversity data is available for this area, the accumulation of data in more frequently sampled regions reveals sampling gaps, especially in deep and remote regions. The ALONGate project studies biodiversity across temporal and spatial gradients and connects data from previously established projects around Iceland (BIOICE: Benthic Invertebrates of Icelandic waters 1992 – 2004 and IceAGE: Icelandic marine Animals: Genetics and Ecology since 2011).

title: About ALONGate
text:
ALONGate Transects
Since 2023, annual Epibenthic Sledge (EBS) sampling in the HAUSGARTEN long-term ecological observatory established by the Alfred-Wegener-Institute contributes to a fundamental understanding of local warm and cold-water species distributions. Samples collected on a latitudinal Nord-South transect from Germany to the Fram Strait fill knowledge gaps for future observations of faunal community shifts towards northern waters.
Additionally, two longitudinal transects, one from Greenland to Svalbard, one from Greenland to Norwegian Sea, are established.



ALONGate transects in the Gateway area. Sampling of the transect No. 1 at Fram Strait is collaborated with annual visit at AWI HAUSGARTEN LTER. Transect No. 3 is the deep-sea complementation to the transect No. 1, hence also called as “deep transect”. Transect No. 2 connects the other transects latitudinally.


In-situ sampling of latitudinal and longitudinal deep-sea transects throughout the Gateway area is complemented with the deployment of long-term Benthic Lander Observatory Systems (BLOS) at critical intersecting nodes of the North-South and East-West transects, with a special focus on collecting image data of Vulnerable Marine Ecosystems (VMEs) like hydrothermal vents or cold-water coral (CWC) reefs across seasonal changes.




Deployed BLOS around Iceland - they are recording the seafloor as you look at this!


Based on the compiled dataset of abiotic (bathymetric assessments, benthic oxygen uptake measurements, sediment samples) and biotic parameters (macrofauna samples, image data), a comprehensive comparison of macro- and megafauna community will contribute to a better understanding of benthic biodiversity and its driving parameters.

title: ALONGate
text:
Carolin Uhlir

Benthic Biogeography, German Centre for Marine Biodiversity Research (DZMB), Senckenberg am Meer • University of Hamburg
carolin.uhlir@senckenberg.de
Benthic sampling, Macrofauna (Cumacea, Pycnogonida)



Having personally experienced the Arctic as a highly dynamic and endangered region on several expeditions, I feel closely connected to its unique ecosystem. The combination of deep-sea and Arctic research fuelled my desire to conduct research in little-explored regions, leading me to start my doctoral studies with the ALONGate project (A Long-term Observatory of the North Atlantic Gateway to the Arctic). Under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Saskia Brix and Prof. Dr. Bodil Bluhm (University of Tromsø), my research examines the taxonomic and genetic diversity of boreal and Arctic deep-sea fauna and the impact of Atlantification. But before we can actually observe and describe shifts, we need to document the current status quo. My taxonomic focus here is on two representatives of benthic macro- and megafauna, the comma crustaceans (Cumacea) and sea spiders (Pantopoda). I am investigating which environmental factors influence their occurrence and how their distribution will change as a result of ocean warming by using DNA barcoding, geographic information systems (GIS), R, species distribution modelling (SDM) and supplementing my data set with publicly available data.

Prof. Dr. Saskia Brix

saskia.brix@uni-hamburg.de
Principle Investigator, Macrofauna (Isopoda)



Prof. Dr. Saskia Brix is a leading deep‑sea researcher whose work reveals the hidden biodiversity of the world’s cold and remote ocean regions. Trained originally as a teacher in biology, history, and education, she later turned her curiosity toward the deep sea and completed her PhD in 2006 on the diversity and evolution of isopods—small crustaceans that play important roles in seafloor ecosystems.
Her scientific journey began on the global stage through the Census of Marine Life (2000–2010), a landmark programme that brought together researchers from around the world to document life in the oceans. Since then, she has taken part in and led major international research efforts and has served as chief scientist on eight deep‑sea expeditions. Many of these missions explored the northern Atlantic and Arctic, regions that are changing rapidly and remain among the least studied on Earth.
Saskia’s research combines classical taxonomy with modern genetic tools to understand how species evolve, spread, and adapt in the deep sea. Her work also connects biodiversity with ecosystem functioning, helping to explain how deep‑sea communities respond to environmental change and why they matter for the health of the planet. This integrative approach formed the basis of her habilitation at the University of Hamburg in 2021.
Beyond research, she plays an active role at the interface of science and policy. She co‑leads the Marine Genetic Resources working group within the Deep Ocean Stewardship Initiative (DOSI) and contributes to international discussions on the protection of marine biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction. She also supports the development of Germany’s marine research infrastructure as co‑lead of the DFG Priority Programme “Research Vessels” (SPP 2520).

title: Cumaceans in the Deep Arctic Ocean
text:
Our team focused on Cumaceans (also called “comma shrimp”), which are small crustaceans that live on and in the seafloor. Over the past 10 years, using gears like box corers and epibenthic sleds, we sampled deep-sea cumaceans living below 500 m depth at the HAUSGARTEN LTER. Nearly 2200 individual specimens were examined for this study and we found:

Cumacean diversity peaks between 1,200 and 1,500 meters deep
Some species live much deeper than previously known, such as Leucon acutirostris diving deeper for astonishing 3511 meters!
We didn’t find any species that only live below 2,000 meters. Instead, most of these species can thrive across a massive range of depths and are widespread across the Arctic.




HAUSGARTEN LTER is located at Fram Strait between Svalbard and Greenland. It is strongly effected by the local current system: West Spitzbergen Current (WSC), East Greenland Current (EGC), and Return Atlantic Current (RAC).

title: Cumaceans in the Deep Arctic Ocean
section: The first identification key for Arctic Cumaceans
text:
The first identification key for Arctic Cumaceans
We’ve put together a comprehensive catalogue featuring simplified traditional and digital identification keys for 64 species of deep-sea Cumacea. Based on our models, this list is likely a complete representation of cumacean species in the Arctic deep sea. Because the Central Arctic Ocean has a low uniqueness of taxa, these identification keys can be reliably applied to the entire deep Arctic Ocean.
We also found some surprising physical traits that challenge how we previously classified certain species (especially in the families Diastylidae and Leuconidae), reminding us that the deep sea always has more to teach us.

title: A Long-term Observatory on the Seafloor
text:
BLOS, stands for Benthic Lander Observatory System, is a customized system designed for data collection on the seafloor for a long period of time. Currently, three of such systems have been successfully deployed around Iceland during the MSM145 expedition in 2026.
Deployed BLOS around Iceland - they are recording the seafloor as you look at this!

title: A Long-term Observatory on the Seafloor
text:
How are they built?
The conceptual design of our BLOS is based on the landers originally constructed by IFREMER. The physical structure consists of stainless steel frames to mount the individual components, including the camera, energy modules, the communication and storage systems. To ensure stable deployment and long-term durability in the extreme deep-sea environment, the equipment housings are constructed from titanium, a material known for its high resistance to immense pressure and saltwater corrosion. Once deployed, the system operates autonomously, programmed to record between 60 and 160 seconds of video every 12 hours. This continuous monitoring cycle will be carried out for an entire year until the next visit to retrieve the data.




dummy




Our engineers Maik (left) and Hauke (right) assemblying BLOS onboard

title: A Long-term Observatory on the Seafloor
text:
Deployment and Recovery
Our BLOS are specifically designed for deployment and recovery using GEOMAR’s ROV Phoca, allowing the entire system to be loaded onto the ROV’s porch in one go and brought to the desired spot on the seafloor. To set up the systems efficiently, we use deep-sea Wi-Fi modules developed by IFREMER.
The ROV and the BLOS each hold a Wi-Fi module that allows real-time data transmission from the BLOS computer to the ROV. Once the ROV reaches the deployment site, the positioning, lighting, and camera configuration are carried out by controlling the BLOS directly from the mission control onboard the vessel. When all settings are complete, the Wi-Fi module linking the BLOS is removed from the ROV container, detaching the two systems completely.

BLOS loaded on ROV Phoca

title: New and Old Isopods
text:
A new isopod species was discovered at the Nidhogg chimney (3016 m) in the Jøtul vent field and the deep-sea Amundsen Basin (4156 m) in the Artic Ocean. Based on the morphological and molecular evidence, a new genus will be erected including the previously described Jaera tyleri Malyutina & Brandt, 2014. Both species from the newly erected genus share a set of traits, that significantly differ from the rest of the typically shallow-water Jaera species. Two of such characters stood out: they were both sampled at abyssal depth, and presumably both feed on bacteria. While J. tyleri was collected on whale bones and grazing on the bacterial community on the bones, the new species were found at an active hydrothermal vent site and presumably feeds on the chemosynthetic bacteria.



CLSM scans of the new isopod species in dorsal and ventral views (Kohlenbach et al., under review)


The necessity of a taxonomic revision of Jaera Leach, 1814 has already been recognized, as well as the enclosing family Janiridae G.O. Sars, 1897, which is proven to be polyphyletic. This study contributes the first step in resolving the systematics of these groups and our understanding to the ecology of isopods inhabiting chemosynthetic environments.



Stations of the sampling campaign, red points indicates the locations where the new species was found (Kohlenbach et al., under review)

title: New and Old Isopods
text:
A new isopod species was discovered at the Nidhogg chimney (3016 m) in the Jøtul vent field and the deep-sea Amundsen Basin (4156 m) in the Artic Ocean. Based on the morphological and molecular evidence, a new genus will be erected including the previously described Jaera tyleri Malyutina & Brandt, 2014. Both species from the newly erected genus share a set of traits, that significantly differ from the rest of the typically shallow-water Jaera species. Two of such characters stood out: they were both sampled at abyssal depth, and presumably both feed on bacteria. While J. tyleri was collected on whale bones and grazing on the bacterial community on the bones, the new species were found at an active hydrothermal vent site and presumably feeds on the chemosynthetic bacteria.



CLSM scans of the new isopod species in dorsal and ventral views (Kohlenbach et al., under review)


The necessity of a taxonomic revision of Jaera Leach, 1814 has already been recognized, as well as the enclosing family Janiridae G.O. Sars, 1897, which is proven to be polyphyletic. This study contributes the first step in resolving the systematics of these groups and our understanding to the ecology of isopods inhabiting chemosynthetic environments.



Stations of the sampling campaign, red points indicates the locations where the new species was found (Kohlenbach et al., under review)

title: New and Old Isopods
text:
Disconectes coxalis Kussakin, 1983
Disconectes coxalis was officially described by Kussakin in 1983, but the type materials was lost later. Adding to the only four individuals collected from Canadian Basins from 3100 to 3400 m depth, approx. 70 specimens of this species were collected at the Eurasian part of the Arctic Ocean during the ArcWatch-1 expedition onboard RV Polarstern, exactly 40 years after the species was described. The newly collected specimens will be used for the re-description along with molecular data.



Map of the Arctic Ocean with the stations of the type locality of Disconectes coxalis (orange) and stations from ArcWatch (PS138) where specimens of Disconectes coxalis were found.


Although being sampled in the central Arctic Ocean, this species has not been found elsewhere, particularly at the HAUSGARTEN LTER in the Fram Strait, which represents the only deep channel connecting Arctic Ocean with other Ocean sectors. Based on this, D. coxalis are suggested to be endemic in the Arctic.
